claims.text: Progressive plastic deformation in FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers under sustained loading is governed by competition between bulk-layer dislocation plasticity and interface-dominated creep mechanisms.
Reducing individual layer thickness increases the relative influence and density of interfaces.
Interfaces in these multilayers act as dislocation sources.
Interfaces in these multilayers also act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Changing individual layer thickness shifts the dominant creep mechanism.
The proposed Al-Cr-Fe-Ni multilayers preserve coherent or semi-coherent interfaces at nanoscale layer thicknesses.
Individual layer thickness modulates interface density and interface quality.
In relatively thick layers, bulk dislocation motion dominates deformation.
Dominance of bulk dislocation motion in thicker layers produces higher creep rates.
Increasing interface density by thinning the layers facilitates dislocation nucleation at layer boundaries.
The increased interface density in thinner layers impedes dislocation pile-ups.
Interface impediment of dislocation pile-ups lowers the creep rate.
Thinner individual layers will have lower creep rates than thicker individual layers.
Thinner individual layers will have greater resistance to progressive plastic deformation than thicker layers.
Interfacial strengthening effects reach a maximum at a critical individual layer thickness.
Outside the proposed critical thickness range, conventional bulk-like creep mechanisms dominate.
The proposed mechanism applies only while the nanoscale multilayers retain coherent or semi-coherent interfaces under sustained loading.
